title: Ecclesiastes 1:1–11
context: The book opens by naming its speaker as the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem, and sounds its keynote: all is vanity. The word WEB renders as vanity is the Hebrew hebel, whose basic sense is vapor or breath; readers take it in this book to suggest what is fleeting, what is insubstantial, or what is enigmatic or even absurd, and the sense may shift with context. The traditional view identifies the Preacher with Solomon; many others read the book as the work of a later author writing in a Solomonic persona. This passage leaves the question open. A poem follows on the endless rounds of generations, sun, wind, and rivers, asking what people gain from their labor under the sun and observing that nothing is new and nothing is remembered.

verses.text: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:
verses.arminianNotes: The book names its speaker as the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the traditional view identifies him with Solomon, while many others see a later author writing in a Solomonic persona.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold both possibilities in view, and many find that the book’s message does not depend on settling authorship. Shared ground: both traditions receive the book as Scripture whoever wrote it, and leave the question open.

verses.text: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Vanity of vanities” is a superlative form, meaning something like utter vanity. Arminian readers note that hebel, rendered vanity, may suggest vapor, breath, or what is fleeting, and that no single English word captures its range.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that others take the word to suggest enigma or even absurdity in certain contexts, and the sense may vary across the book. Shared ground: both traditions resist reducing the refrain to one slogan or to simple despair.

verses.text: What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher asks what people gain from all their labor under the sun. Arminian readers see an honest question about the lasting value of human effort when viewed only within this world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “under the sun” as framing the book’s inquiry as observation of life in this world. Both traditions read the question as opening an exploration that the book will pursue, rather than giving a final answer here.

verses.text: One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Generations come and go, but the earth remains. Arminian readers note the contrast between the brevity of human life and the stability of the created order, which outlasts each generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verse a sober reminder of human transience before God’s enduring creation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing human striving within the larger and longer rhythms of the world.

verses.text: The sun also rises, and the sun goes down, and hurries to its place where it rises.
verses.arminianNotes: The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to where it rises. Arminian readers note the image of the sun’s daily round, which some read as tireless and others as wearying repetition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sun’s regular course as an example of the order God placed in creation, though the Preacher stresses its sameness. Both traditions read the verse as part of a poem about cycles that seem to go nowhere.

verses.text: The wind goes toward the south, and turns around to the north. It turns around continually as it goes, and the wind returns again to its courses.
verses.arminianNotes: The wind blows south, turns north, and circles back on its courses. Arminian readers note that the poem moves from sun to wind to rivers, building a picture of ceaseless motion without arrival.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wind’s circling as a vivid picture of activity that returns to where it began. Shared ground: the image serves the poem’s point about repetition, and both traditions read it as observation rather than science.

verses.text: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.
verses.arminianNotes: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is never full. Arminian readers note the paradox of constant flow without fulfillment, which mirrors the restlessness of human desire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rivers’ unending course as illustrating the Preacher’s point that labor does not reach a final rest under the sun. Both traditions read the verse as poetry drawn from the observed world.

verses.text: All things are full of weariness beyond uttering. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
verses.arminianNotes: All things are full of weariness beyond words, and the eye and ear are never satisfied. Arminian readers see the restlessness of human longing, which no amount of seeing or hearing can fill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing the limits of what creation alone can give the human heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the dissatisfaction as an honest observation that the book explores, not a rejection of God’s world.

verses.text: That which has been is that which shall be, and that which has been done is that which shall be done; and there is no new thing under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes: What has been will be, and there is nothing new under the sun. Arminian readers note that the Preacher speaks of patterns of human experience, not that no new event or invention can occur.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing the sameness of the human condition across generations. Both traditions read the saying within its poetic setting, as a reflection on repetition in life under the sun.

verses.text: Is there a thing of which it may be said, “Behold, this is new”? It has been long ago, in the ages which were before us.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher asks whether anything can be called new, and answers that it existed long ago. Arminian readers note that apparent novelty often turns out to be a return of what earlier generations already knew.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as humbling the human tendency to think one’s own age unique. Shared ground: the verse restates the point of 1:9 in a question, and both traditions read it as wisdom about human limits.

verses.text: There is no memory of the former; neither shall there be any memory of the latter that are to come, among those that shall come after.
verses.arminianNotes: There is no memory of former generations, and later ones will also be forgotten. Arminian readers see a sobering reflection on how quickly human achievements and names fade from memory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as preparing for the book’s later reflections on death and forgetting (compare 2:16). Both traditions read it as an observation about life under the sun, which the book will set beside the fear of God.
